title: re:vision – A community-driven replication initiative for condition-rich neuroscience of visually-presented stimuli
abstract:
Condition-rich fMRI studies have contributed strongly to our understanding of visual representations in the brain and their alignment with deep neural networks. However, the datasets underlying these studies often capture only a fraction of visual experience or may undersample important parts of the visual world. This raises questions about the replicability and generalizability of these findings.
To address this challenge, we introduce re:vision, a community-driven initiative that aims to systematically replicate influential findings in the neuroscience of visually presented images to determine the degree to which the field reflects genuine findings beyond dataset-specific biases. re:vision is built on LAION-fMRI, a new multi-echo 7T fMRI dataset in which, over >30 sessions, five participants each viewed approximately 7,000 images selected to maximize coverage of visual and semantic space. In re:vision, researchers will replicate published studies following original analysis procedures as closely as possible. Beyond replication, the initiative aims to test generalization using out-of-distribution images and semantically defined subsets of the stimulus space. Through large-scale collaborative replication on a carefully constructed dataset, re:vision aims to establish a stronger empirical foundation for visual neuroscience and NeuroAI.

title: Recent Trial History Improves Encoding Models of Brain Responses During Emotional Video Viewing
abstract: Trial-wise brain responses during naturalistic viewing may depend not only on features of the current trial but also on recent stimulus history. Here, we investigated whether adding recent-trial information improves region-wise encoding models of trial-wise fMRI responses during emotional video viewing. Focusing primarily on emotion features, we compared current-only models with history-augmented models that incorporated 1-back and 2-back information, while also examining visual feature spaces in parallel. Adding 1-back features improved prediction across much of cortex and many subcortical regions, with the strongest gains observed for emotion features. Visual feature spaces also showed positive 1-back gains, but these were smaller. By contrast, adding 2-back features produced little further improvement beyond the 1-back model. These results indicate that trial-wise responses during emotional video viewing are not fully captured by current-trial features alone and that the most useful recent-history information is concentrated in the immediately preceding trial, particularly in the emotion feature space.

title: How RNNs shape the geometry of mixture inputs? Biased suppression and emergent codes stem from connectivity
abstract:
Neural circuits routinely process mixtures --- weighted combinations of simpler inputs.
Examples include plaids in vision, competing speakers in audition, odor blends in olfaction.
Empirically, the response to such mixtures can either combine the component responses proportionally,
or suppress one in favor of the other, or encode new directions that neither component alone produces \citep{Rust2006,Busse2009,Zoccolan2005}.
Which circuit properties determine which encoding arises?
The Divisive Normalization model captures the phenomenology of proportional and suppressive regimes,
but does not explain the underlying mechanisms, nor does it predict emergent mixture-selective directions.

This study shows how all three encoding geometries arise from a single mechanism in a biologically plausible network model: recurrent connectivity amplifies different directions of activity non-uniformly.
A mixture input shifts the network's operating point relative to each single stimulus, and this shift rescales each dynamical mode by a different factor.
Depending on the connectivity structure, this non-uniform rescaling can bias the mixture response toward one component or generate new encoding directions not reducible to any combination of single-stimulus responses.

Thus, in recurrent networks, the same stimulus family can be linearly mixed, selected, or segregated in the encoding space,
and this geometry can flexibly change with the stimulus itself. Mixture processing is a non-trivial computation, which has implications for downstream systems.

title: Adaptive Distortions of Confidence Reflect Environment Statistics and Internal Constraints
abstract: Confidence judgements are widely modelled as reflecting the strength of internal evidence, yet this account rests on SDT frameworks that assume static, symmetric decision environments. Although evidence reliability and natural input statistics can independently bias confidence (Boldt et al., 2017; Webb et al., 2023), how category priors and evidence variance jointly distort confidence towards accuracy correspondence remains unknown. Here, we manipulate category priors and evidence variance in SDT simulations while holding d’ constant. Skewed priors shift the decision criterion towards the frequent category, producing category-specific distortions in metacognitive sensitivity (AUROC2) without altering discrimination performance. Feedforward neural networks trained on MNIST digits and Gabor patches under unbalanced category frequencies develop the same asymmetric confidence patterns while maintaining classification accuracy, demonstrating that these distortions can emerge from optimisation dynamics alone, without explicit criterion computation. Our findings indicate that metacognitive precision is jointly shaped by environmental statistics and decision-policy optimisation.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+theoretical / computational neuroscience

title: A Modular Framework for Embedding Brain-like Topology in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Spatially embedded recurrent neural networks (seRNNs) provide a framework for investigating how the brain’s spatial organisation shapes computation. Previous work extended this framework to include topological constraints, using the Earth Mover’s Distance between communicability distributions to drive artificial networks toward brain-like connectivity structure. A proof of concept demonstrated that such networks not only converge toward empirical communicability distributions but also develop spatially structured mixed selectivity for distinct cognitive demands — a functional signature absent in unconstrained networks. However, this initial demonstration required manual tuning and was limited to a single topological measure and task. Here we present a modular framework designed for the systematic investigation of how different structural properties of biological neural networks affect learning and computation. We present functional results from the original proof of concept, describe the framework’s design, and discuss how this approach enables controlled investigation of which topological properties of the brain matter for which computations.

title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio Predicts Neural Response Predictability with Limited Association with Tuning Properties in Mouse Visual Cortex
abstract:
What determines whether a neuron's activity can be accurately predicted 
by a deep neural network (DNN)? The field commonly assumes that neurons 
with strong, reliable responses are the most predictable. Here, we 
challenge this assumption by dissecting neural responses into signal and 
noise components using large-scale calcium imaging data from mouse visual 
cortex ($N = 78,853$ neurons). Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR; Spearman 
$\rho = 0.552$), rather than total response power ($\rho = 0.310$), is 
the dominant predictor of DNN prediction performance (trial-averaged 
correlation). Furthermore, we identify a population of neurons with high 
trial-to-trial variability but high signal power that achieves superior 
comparable predictability (mean performance $0.401$), challenging the view that high 
variability necessarily degrades encoding fidelity. This work establishes 
SNR as a principled metric for neuron selection in neural encoding 
models.

title: Belief Filtering: Meta-inference of Internal Models
abstract: Characterising the internal states underlying behaviour is challenging.  Human participants or other "agents" may act rationally, but with beliefs shaped by mistaken models of the causal structure of the environment and by internal noise.  External "observers" may access a veridical world state and witness behaviour, but have no direct view of beliefs, noise, or the internal model that shapes them.  Here, we demonstrate a formal framework to clearly distinguish agent and observer models, and their belief states, within an amortised meta-inference approach.  The approach makes it possible to track the evolution of an agent's beliefs across time, and thus identify the internal model on which it acts.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+theoretical / computational neuroscience

title: Spatial uncertainty underlies geometric distortions in navigation and grid cell tuning
abstract:
Navigation requires estimating one’s location from noisy sensory inputs. While environmental geometry is known to distort both navigational behavior and grid cell responses, these effects have been explained piecemeal. Here we propose a unifying principle: the brain maintains and updates uncertainty about spatial location, and this uncertainty shapes both behavior and neural coding.

We introduce the Bayesian Image-computable Observer for Navigation (BION) that integrates visual and self-motion inputs to infer a posterior over location. Crucially, spatial uncertainty is structured by environmental geometry due to retinal projection, yielding systematic inhomogeneities in information. These in turn explain human homing across trapezoidal, stretched, and compressed
environments. 

We further show that encoding this uncertainty in neural population codes predicts rat grid field size, anisotropy, rescaling, and boundary-tethering under analogous manipula-
tions. Unlike prior models that treat distortions as epiphenomena, our framework interprets them as optimal adaptations to uncertainty.

These results suggest that spatial uncertainty is not incidental but fundamental to navigation, providing a normative account linking perception, behavior, and neural representation.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+theoretical / computational neuroscience

title: Experienced dimensions of 3D scene structure provide organizing dimensions for scene-selective areas in the human brain
abstract: Here, we explore how natural visual experience of scenes is related to the representation of 3D scene structure in the human brain. First, we define a model to quantify 3D scene structure in terms of the distribution of surface normals and distances in arbitrary images. To quantify natural visual experience of these 3D structural features, we apply this model to samples of egocentric video frames drawn from a large database of head-mounted video collected while human subjects performed natural tasks. We then use principal components analysis to discover commonly experienced patterns of 3D structural features. We find that the first dimension of variance in scene structure distinguishes open from closed scenes. To relate visual experience of structure to brain responses, we model brain responses in the Natural Scenes Dataset as a function of the same 3D structural features. Analysis of fit model weights reveals a gradient of selectivity from open to closed scenes across multiple scene-selective areas. Thus, the main dimension that varies in our visual experience of scenes is mapped across scene-selective areas in the human brain.

title: Sensorimotor context modulates reinforcement learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning, a framework for human learning and decision-making, is influenced by a wide array of factors. One underexplored domain is sensorimotor context. This study examined behavior on a two-choice reversal learning task under two conditions: stationary (arm movements between parallel computers) and active (walking between computers). Participants chose repeatedly between two options rewarding at 70% and 30% probability, with the advantageous option reversing with 20% probability every 15 trials. A mixed-effects model revealed that sensorimotor context modulated reinforcement learning, but only in participants who completed the active condition first: the probability of repeating the same choice was higher in the subsequent stationary trials. No such effect emerged in the stationary-first group. Further work will use computational modeling, affective states, and strategy reports to identify the specific mechanisms.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+psychological / behavioral research

title: Mode-Selective Memory Decay from Multilayer Neural Architecture: A Spectral Theory
abstract: Detailed episodic memories decay faster than schematic representations across behavioral, neuroimaging, and lesion paradigms, yet no formal model derives this rate separation from neural architecture. Complementary learning systems theory explains where fast and slow memories reside but not why their decay rates differ quantitatively. Spaced repetition models fit forgetting curves empirically but lack a mechanistic substrate. This paper introduces a spectral framework that formalizes memory as controlled state evolution on a product cognitive manifold equipped with a multilayer graph Laplacian. The Kronecker-sum structure of this Laplacian yields an additive eigenvalue decomposition in which high-frequency modes (encoding fine-grained perceptual detail) decay exponentially faster than low-frequency modes (encoding broad relational structure). The spectral gap of the weakest layer sets the global forgetting rate, producing a layer-bottleneck principle. A stability bound constrains how strongly intervention can perturb the system before reconsolidation-like overwrite occurs. Each operator component maps onto identified neural mechanisms, including hippocampal binding, neocortical consolidation, thalamic gating, and amygdala salience tagging. The framework predicts mode-selective decay, layer bottlenecking, load-sensitive forgetting, and reconsolidation margin violation, all of which align with established empirical findings. The Weibull forgetting curve emerges naturally as a consequence of multi-mode projection, and the spectral gap bounds the mutual information decay rate between the current and initial cognitive state. Preliminary validation from a deployed adaptive learning plat33 form (1,500+ users, 4,200 review events) supports the derived relationship between knowledge-graph spectral gap and observed retention (r=0.71, p<0.001). These results suggest that the detail-before-schema decay ordering is not an empirical regularity requiring fitting but a mathematical consequence of multilayer architecture, opening a path toward spectral methods as a unifying formalism across behavioral and neural levels of memory analysis.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+psychological / behavioral research+theoretical / computational neuroscience+experimental neuroscience (systems / cognitive)

title: CogMaze: A Benchmark of Egocentric Spatial Understanding in Humans and Vision-Language Models
abstract: Humans are adept at spatial understanding: integrating egocentric observations to support navigation and reasoning. Evidence suggests this relies on an allocentric representation of the environment (cognitive maps). While vision-language models (VLMs) perform well on many multimodal tasks, they remain weak at spatial understanding, suggesting they don't form cognitive map-like representations. We introduce CogMaze, a benchmark of spatial understanding in humans and VLMs. It includes a 3D simulated maze with visual landmarks, a ground-truth schema for probing representations, and tasks for humans and VLMs. We evaluate with a VLM in environments of varying complexity.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+psychological / behavioral research

title: Human Causal Reasoning Demonstrates Neurosymbolic Structure in Exploration-driven Benchmarks
abstract: Studying how humans navigate sparse-reward environments may reveal architectural principles for more flexible AI, as human cognition excels where AI systems continue to struggle: in causal inference, learning from sparse data, and flexible problem-solving. To investigate this, 40 participants solved two instruction-less puzzle benchmarks with five levels each. Verbal reasoning traces were elicited using a think-aloud protocol; keystrokes, timestamps, and game states were logged as participants navigated the puzzles. Through grounded theory analysis of behavioral observations, verbal markers were tracked across trajectories of mechanic-based and objective-based learning, and then classified into a taxonomy of knowledge acquisition using natural language processing for feature extraction. Findings reveal the structured inferential processes of human learning, challenging the sufficiency of the traditional explore-exploit framework and motivating neurosymbolic architectures capable of genuine causal learning in sparse-reward, exploration-driven environments. We introduce 'establish' as a novel intermediary mechanism capturing the hypothesis-testing and confirmatory behaviors that bridge exploration and exploitation in computational learning models.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling

title: Meta-learning In-Context Enables Training-Free Cross Subject Decoding of Vision and Motor
abstract: Decoding neural representations across both visual and motor domains is fundamentally constrained by structural and functional inter-subject variability. Current methodologies typically require subject-specific training or gradient-based fine-tuning to account for individualized cortical organization. To address this limitation, we propose a meta-learning in-context framework that enables training-free cross-subject decoding. The model operates through a hierarchical inference process. First, it performs system identification by conditioning on a limited set of paired behavioral and neural data from a target individual, inferring voxel-specific forward encoding models. Second, the architecture aggregates these estimated encoder weights alongside observed neural activations across distributed cortical regions to execute functional inversion. This formulation predicts unseen visual stimuli and motor targets for novel subjects without requiring parametric updates, anatomical coregistration, or shared calibration datasets. By framing neural translation as an in-context learning objective, this approach demonstrates how generalized inverse models can scale across heterogeneous neural datasets and diverse sensorimotor applications.

title: Escape Response Reveals Computations Of Network Robustness
abstract: Whole-brain imaging in C. elegans with optogenetic stimulation of a few neurons that induce the escape response provides a comprehensive understanding of how the network achieves this robust behavior. With the advent of high-speed calcium imaging through Bessel illumination, we demonstrate that neurons with earliest onsets are not necessarily those directly anatomically connected to simulated neurons.

title: Geometric regularization of representation spaces enables efficient application of cognitive operators
abstract:
Humans solve many cognitive tasks by applying operators to internal representations rather than directly manipulating sensory input. A central challenge for artificial agents is to reach human-level generalization on abstract problems. One idea is to learn latent representation spaces whose geometric structure supports the efficient learning, application and generalization of operators \citep{marchetti2023equivariant, van2020plannable}. We refer to this kind of operator as a cognitive operator.
In this work, we study how the curvature of representation spaces influences the learnability and accuracy of cognitive operators corresponding to structured environmental transformations. Focusing on the mental rotation task, we model an agent using an encoder whose latent space serves as an internal representation. Drawing on tools from differential geometry, we formalize environmental transformations as Lie group actions and cognitive operators as vector fields on a latent manifold. Motivated by curvature-dependent error bounds for differential equations on Riemannian manifolds, we propose a set of curvature-regularization objectives that encourage locally linear, low-curvature latent geometries.
Experimental results on synthetic mental rotation stimuli show that curvature-regularized latent spaces yield more accurate operator learning performance. Together, these findings highlight the importance of latent geometry for bridging representation learning and cognitive computation, and provide a principled framework for learning cognitive operators in neural systems.

title: Understanding and Optimizing Contrastive Hebbian Learning Through Dynamical System Analysis
abstract: Contrastive Hebbian Learning (CHL), a dynamical system algorithm inspired from Hebb’s Rule, neurons that fire together wire together, is a local rule that requires no global feedback and aligns with brain inspired networks. Current implementations rely on fixed settling steps for integration to reach equilibrium. In this work we investigate the dynamical system of CHL to provide an objective method for quantifying settling time. By analyzing the layers trajectories, we can demonstrate that the network behaves as a stable linear differential equation with hidden layers converging to stable nodes, which can be analyzed mathematically. By quantifying the number of steps, we can show using CIFAR-10 and MNIST that we can provide a control mechanism for cutting training time iterations compared to fixed steps CHL models.

title: Interactions Between Features and Conjunctions during Category Learning
abstract: In learning multi-feature categories, humans often rely on primary features themselves rather than conjunction of these features. Conjunctions have also been recognized as critical for learning complex tasks, as conjunctions can expand the dimensionality of neural representations to allow for linear classification of categories which are nonlinear in the primary features (e.g. XOR). When humans learn a task requiring use of both feature and conjunctive information, it remains unclear how feature and conjunctive contributions to choice behavior interact across the learning trajectory. Here, we investigate the interactions between feature and conjunctive representations with a task in which humans learn categories from stimuli composed of fractal images at three spatially defined features. We develop a kernel-based framework to decompose behavioral choices into contributions from feature and conjunctive learning modes. The decomposed learning dynamics showed three intriguing interactions in learning of features and conjunctions within a task block: (i) anti-correlation between loadings of primary features; (ii) enhanced loading of a conjunction yoked to a highly loaded primary feature; and (iii) reduced loading of a conjunction not yoked to that primary feature. Furthermore, we tested how learning the relative ‘weights’ of different features transfers from one task block to the next block, which requires learning new categories from new fractals presented at the same spatial feature locations. High loading on a conjunction during the prior block led to enhanced learning of a yoked primary feature during the subsequent block. We found that multiple prominent category-learning models fail to capture all four interactions observed in our experiments. Finally, eye-tracking during task performance implicates spatial attentional mechanisms in mediating these feature interactions. Together, our findings reveal multiple forms of interaction between primary and conjunctive features during category learning, which poses constraints for future models of learning, and its interplay with attention, in multi-feature environments.
secondary_area: psychological / behavioral research+theoretical / computational neuroscience+experimental neuroscience (systems / cognitive)

title: Bottom-up Modeling of Striatum and its Brain Circuit Interactions
abstract: The basal ganglia is involved in a variety of cognitive functions such as action selection, goal-directed behavior, and reward-based decision-making. However, most computational models of the cortico-basal ganglia circuits exclude major characteristics such as detailed physiological interactions among cells, and inclusion of multiple distinct cell types (including GABAergic fast spiking neurons, cholinergic interneurons, and more). Given the extensive role of these interneurons in reward-based learning, it is of great interest to study their  properties at the circuit level. Here we present a bottom-up biologically-derived spiking model of the cortico-basal ganglia circuit incorporating D1 and D2 medium spiny neurons as well as fast-spiking and cholinergic  interneurons, and evaluate it on a dot-distortion category-learning task matched to macaque electrophysiology and rodent interneuron recordings. The model reproduces key empirical signatures including task-dependent firing patterns and cell-type-specific interactions across striatal and prefrontal cortical populations. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating multiple populations of existing cell types into computational models of brain circuitry.  The model offers new insights into the circuit-level mechanisms of reward-based decision-making.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+experimental neuroscience (systems / cognitive)

title: Persistent polar-angle asymmetries in performance and system-level computations despite equating cortical size
abstract: Visual performance is location-dependent: Typically, it decreases with eccentricity and is higher along the horizontal than the vertical meridian–termed the horizontal-vertical anisotropy (HVA)–and along the lower- than the upper-vertical meridian–vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA). We have previously studied how (i) system-level computations vary across the visual field: Internal noise increases with eccentricity and gain varies around polar angle, yielding both an HVA and VMA, and (ii) cortical surface area modulates performance: equating cortical size (M-scaling) eliminates contrast threshold differences across eccentricity, but only reduces polar angle asymmetries. Here, we investigated whether and how scaling stimulus size to equate cortical surface area across locations (M-scaling)—on a per individual basis—modulates performance and system-level computations. To do so, we estimated contrast thresholds using an equivalent-noise protocol (signal embedded in varying noise levels), and fit a perceptual template model to estimate gain and internal noise at each location, using both constant and M-scaled stimulus sizes. Across eccentricity, internal noise increased when stimulus size was constant. M-scaling eliminated this eccentricity effect by equating internal noise, while gain increased in the periphery. Around polar angle, gain was higher at the horizontal than the vertical meridian and at the lower- than the upper-vertical meridian, but internal noise did not vary. M-scaling diminished the HVA in gain and resulted in a VMA in internal noise. These results indicate that visual performance differences across eccentricity and around polar angle reflect different computations: the former in internal noise and the latter in gain. Critically, equating cortical surface area across locations on an individual basis eliminates eccentricity differences, but polar angle asymmetries in performance and system-level computations persist, albeit in an attenuated manner.

title: Diffusion-map phenotyping from exactly solvable brain-dynamics models via descriptor-family kernel fusion
abstract: Comparing brain dynamics across heterogeneous subjects requires representations that are cross-subject comparable, mechanistically interpretable, and compact for unsupervised phenotyping. We present a pipeline integrating consensus shared latent coordinates, exactly solvable pairwise maximum-entropy (Ising) models, and multi-view kernel learning to produce a low-dimensional mechanistic phenotyping space. Whole-brain time series are projected into population-universal shared coordinates by aligning and fusing complementary methods (SRM, MCCA, Group PCA/ICA) via Procrustes rotation and stability-aware consensus weighting. With K=12 shared dimensions, the 2^K=4096 state space permits exact partition-function computation, yielding normalised, directly comparable energy landscapes. Energy-landscape and phase-diagram analyses extract heterogeneous per-subject mechanistic descriptors: attractor structure, barrier spectra, kinetic summaries, and near-criticality observables. We integrate these descriptor families via type-specific similarity kernels (Wasserstein for distributions, radial-basis for scalars, spectral for matrices), combined through multiple kernel learning. Diffusion-map embedding of the fused kernel produces interpretable axes along which subjects are positioned by their full dynamical profile. On resting-state functional ultrasound data from heterogeneous autism-model mice, stable subtype clustering emerges along axes reflecting switching kinetics, landscape ruggedness, and criticality proximity, robust under ablation and bootstrap resampling. The framework supports mechanistic phenotyping when large-sample designs are impractical.

title: Folk Psychological Structure of Mind in Large Language Models
abstract: Humans organize mind perception along two dimensions: Experience (capacity to feel) and Agency (capacity to act and plan), shaping moral judgment, social interaction, and communication. This study adapts Gray, Gray, and Wegner's (2007) mind perception survey to six instruction-tuned LLMs from four architectural families. Behaviorally, most models produce entity rankings on Experience and Agency that significantly correlate with human data. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) of internal activations reveals that folk-psychological structure emerges in intermediate transformer layers even absent any mind-attribution task, with significant alignment in four of six models. These findings suggest that LLMs have internalized an implicit folk psychology reflected in both their overt judgments and internal representations.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+psychological / behavioral research

title: Back to the Feature: Toward a Feature-Centric Account of Brain–LM Alignment
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful proxies for linguistic processing in the human brain, yet the standard practice of quantifying this alignment via a single scalar obscures the underlying drivers of the relationship. This "scalar-centric" approach treats high-dimensional embeddings as atomic units, establishing that alignment exists while remaining agnostic to how it is achieved. We propose a shift toward a feature-centric perspective that inspects the specific embedding dimensions contributing to neural alignment. We demonstrate that while naive feature analyses suggest a superficial homogeneity across the brain, this is a methodological artifact. By synergizing feature decomposition via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) with sparse encoding models (Lasso), we uncover distinct feature subsets that dissociate between cortical regions and temporal windows. We redefine brain-LLM alignment not as aggregate similarity, but as a structural inquiry into which computational dimensions map onto distinct neural dynamics.
secondary_area: artificial intelligence / machine learning+computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling

title: Neuroscience-Inspired Analyses of Visual Interestingness in Multimodal Transformers
abstract:
Human attention is the gateway to conscious perception, memory and decision-making. However, its role in modern transformer models remains largely unexplored. As these systems increasingly influence what people see, prefer and buy, the question arises as to whether they encode principles of human interest or merely exploit large-scale correlations. Addressing this issue is crucial for understanding cognition and ensuring the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in communication and marketing.
In order to address this issue, the concept of visual interest was examined within the multimodal vision-language-model Qwen3-VL-8B, using a pre-defined Common Interestingness (CI) score derived from large-scale human engagement data on the photo-sharing platform Flickr.
In the present study, we analyzed internal representations across vision and language components using methods from the neurosciences. Our analyses revealed that CI information is linearly decodable from final-layer embeddings, indicating that it is encoded in a human-aligned manner.
Dimensionality reduction and Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV) analyses demonstrate that CI-related hidden presentations emerge in intermediate vision transformer layers and becomes progressively more distinguishable across language model layers. Concept vectors derived using geometric, probe, and Sparse Auto-Encoder (SAE) based methods converge in higher layers, as confirmed by representational similarity analysis. This indicates a robust and structured encoding of visual interestingness without explicit supervision.
In particular, we find that human visual interestingness emerges as a structured, linearly accessible representation in multimodal transformers, becoming progressively stronger from visual perception to semantic/language-level processing.
To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to apply systems neuroscience methods to multimodal transformer models in order to study how visual interest is internally represented. Future work will seek to identify shared computational principles linking human brain dynamics and transformer architectures, with the ultimate goal of uncovering the organizing mechanisms — potentially reflecting shared or platonic representational structures — that give rise to attention and interest in both biological and artificial systems.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+psychological / behavioral research

title: Learning Long-Range Temporal Dependencies Through Sleep-Inspired Acceleration
abstract: Learning long-range dependencies between events spread out in time remains difficult for systems constrained by finite memory, posing a central challenge for continual learning systems. In biological neural networks, the temporal scaffolding hypothesis asserts that memory replay during slow-wave sleep functionally reduces the temporal distance between associated events, facilitating novel associations to emerge in subsequent processing. Inspired by this principle, we investigate whether accelerating the propagation of sequential data during learning can improve learning across long horizons. We introduce a hierarchical reservoir architecture with two distinct learning phases. A replay-like phase with controlled temporal acceleration, during which an autoencoder learns compressed representations of reservoir activity, and a supervised phase in which a readout layer is trained to optimize task-specific objectives. We evaluate this approach on a synthetic inference task that requires prediction of future states conditioned on events occurring far in the past, as well as ECG classification of heart beats and rhythms. These results suggest that learning from temporally accelerated sequences provides a complementary mechanism for extending effective memory depth beyond the inherent context window and can be integrated with existing learning rules.

title: Shallow Hippocampal Anticipation and Dopamine Responses During Evaluation of Novel Shortcuts
abstract:
When animals encounter new paths (offering potential shortcuts), they must assess whether the opportunity is worth pursuing. This evaluation likely involves mental simulation over candidate paths, but the specific computations and their neural mechanisms remain unclear. A key computational challenge is that exhaustive search is expensive; the brain may instead use truncated search, simulating a few steps ahead and substituting cached values of intermediate locations instead of extended trajectories.

We investigated these mechanisms using simultaneous recordings of nucleus accumbens dopamine (fiber photometry) and dorsal CA1 hippocampal activity (high-density electrophysiology) in rats navigating a dynamic hexagonal maze where barriers periodically changed location. Previous work reported phasic dopamine excitation upon encountering newly available paths, which was sensitive to aspects of the path's value, but arose rapidly, before animals could have learned value through direct experience. Here, we examine hippocampal representations during this period, testing whether nonlocal activity might subserve forward search and reveal its spatial extent.

Positions decoded from hippocampus at new path encounters were biased toward locations ahead of the animal, particularly on trials where rats subsequently entered the new path. Critically, these representations primarily targeted nearby locations, inside and immediately beyond the new opening, with minimal representation of distant goals. Dopamine responses aligned with decoded hippocampal dynamics showed good alignment with the time when hippocampus first represented the location immediately beyond the new opening (the adjacent hexagon), the nearest location where cached value about subsequent goals might be available. Supporting this interpretation, dopaminergic responses were larger when this adjacent hexagon was visited during reward foraging in the preceding block.

These findings provide preliminary evidence that hippocampal prospective coding accompanies rapid evaluation of new spatial opportunities, suggesting that rather than representing extended trajectories to goals, the brain may judiciously evaluate nearby locations whose cached value can substitute for further search.
secondary_area: computational cognitive science / cognitive modeling+psychological / behavioral research

title: A Probe-Based Detector Using Saliency Divergence, Gradients, and Layer Sensitivity
abstract:
Adversarial patches cause targeted misclassification by steering a model’s evidence toward a small, visible region while human perception remains largely unaffected. We propose a post hoc detector that attaches lightweight probes to a frozen classifier and fuses three complementary signals: (i) input-gradient statistics of the predicted class, (ii) layer-wise sensitivity to small activation noise, and (iii) human-model saliency divergence, quantified by comparing Grad-CAM with human saliency maps. Features from these probes are fed to a small secondary classifier (detector) that predicts whether an input is patched. To our knowledge, our detector is the first adversarial-patch detector to explicitly incorporate human attention modeling via saliency divergence, aligning what the model relies on with where humans look, without modifying or retraining the base model.

Across CAT2000, FIGRIM, and SALICON, using ResNet-50 and EfficientNet-B0 backbones, our detector achieves F1 scores up to 99.6% and remains in the 80–99% range across the adversarial patch attack settings, outperforming probing baselines, SentiNet, and X-Detect. Ablations show gains from adding gradients and divergence to sensitivity in most of the cases, indicating complementary cues and highlighting divergence’s discriminative power. Our detector is simple to deploy (post hoc; no retraining) and provides interpretable rationales via its saliency and sensitivity components, suggesting a practical path to robust, explainable detection of adversarial patches.

title: Circuit motifs underlying representational untangling
abstract: The ventral stream maps patterns of light to increasingly untangled, high-level category representations through hierarchical processing. What circuitry supports this untangling? Here we address this question in a fully observable “model organism,” AlexNet, by extracting the minimal inter-layer wiring sufficient to preserve accurate object categorization. Building on importance-based circuit pruning Hamblin et al., 2022, we refine logit-targeted pruning with (i) \textbf{sign-aware pruning}, which prunes excitatory and inhibitory connections on interleaved schedules to stabilize selection, and (ii) a \textbf{cross-layer marginal-loss} rule that allocates pruning across layers according to the increase in a calibrated one-vs-all loss per removed connection. Across 1,000 ImageNet categories, the resulting decision-preserving circuits retain only ~4.5% of connections and are, on average, ~5.7% below the calibrated unpruned baseline on corrected one-vs-all accuracy. Circuit structure reveals a shared macro-motif: dense early connectivity, progressively sparser convolutional stages, and dramatic sparsity in the fully connected readout. Cross-category wiring overlap also declines across the hierarchy, yet late-stage overlap remains significantly more structured than chance given matched circuit sparsity. At the superordinate level, the animate and inanimate domains contain substantially more shared computational routes within domain than the random a priori expectation, with increasingly separable circuitry along the hierarchy. Broadly, this method exposes the circuit-level computational structure underlying representational untangling, revealing systematic routing motifs across the hierarchy, and providing a computational approach for mapping category-computing circuitry across deep neural network systems.

title: Metacognitive sensitivity governs resource-rational compression in hierarchical structure learning
abstract:
Humans form compressed hierarchical representations and metacognitively evaluate their own uncertainty to cope with information-processing constraints. Computationally, successor representations (SRs) characterize compressed predictive representations of multi-scale environmental structures where states are encoded in terms of their relationships with other states. SR approaches recover a discount factor (𝛾) indexing the temporal horizon of successors, and the contribution of the representation to decisions (𝛽). However, it is unknown how hierarchical structure, coupled with metacognitive evaluation, jointly affect predictive representations and their influence
on behavior. Furthermore, a rational agent should calibrate both aspects described by this framework (𝛾 and 𝛽) not only to environmental statistics, but also to their working memory (WM) capacity. Notably, unfamiliar stimuli require more WM resources for encoding, but it is further unknown if such stimulus-driven WM capacity leads to more compressed representations that blend, rather than distinctly represent, multiple environmental structures. To address these gaps, we fit an analytical SR model to choice behavior from a hierarchical learning paradigm where participants learned co-occurrences embedded in a sequence across two sessions with either familiar line
drawings or unfamiliar fractal stimuli. We found a tradeoff between the discount factor (𝛾 ; representing the degree of compression) and the influence of representations on decisions (𝛽): fractals elicited a greater 𝛾, but line drawings drove higher likelihood of representations influencing choices, suggesting that fractal-induced reductions in available WM capacity may drive greater compression of
structure representations. Further, fractal stimuli elicited a negative relationship between metacognitive sensitivity and discount factor (𝛾), but a positive relationship between metacognitive sensitivity and behavioral dependence on SR (𝛽). We interpret this as evidence that
higher metacognitive sensitivity may support “resource-rational” representational compression and use of efficient internal representations of hierarchical environmental structure.

title: Modeling Visual Cortex by Maximizing Layerwise Multiscale Manifold Capacity
abstract:
Task-optimized deep neural networks have risen to prominence as the most predictive phenomenological models of responses in primate visual cortex, but leave much to be desired from the perspective of biological plausibility.
One such limitation is the reliance on precise credit assignment through global backpropagation of error signals.
Recent work has shown that this weakness can be circumvented by requiring each subsequent stage to solve a distinct and increasingly complex task, allowing for layerwise local learning signals.
We propose a novel strategy for crafting such intermediate losses that uses an efficient coding framework formulated in terms of manifold capacity, which can be computed using a sequence of *canonical cortical computations*.
In particular, we leverage the relationship between the multiscale nature of visual signals and the dilation of receptive field sizes in cascaded visual representations to modulate complexity, allowing for the reapplication of these common loss computations at each stage of the hierarchy.
We evaluate our approach on its ability to predict neural datasets spanning three areas of the ventral stream hierarchy in macaques, as well as human psychophysical data on an object classification task.  We find that our unsupervised layerwise model matches or exceeds the performance of competitive architecture-matched baselines on all evaluations considered.

title: From Clicks to Conflict: A Computational Study of Approach-Avoidance Conflict Task Engagement
abstract:
Approach–avoidance conflicts (AACs), in which the same action entails both appetitive and aversive aspects, are ubiquitous in everyday decision making. Excessive and costly avoidance in such conflicts is a key feature of anxiety disorders, yet the computational mechanisms underlying maladaptive avoidance remain poorly understood. To address this, we adapted a foraging-based AAC paradigm in which participants actively explore visual search fields for rewards while simultaneously being at risk of receiving punishment. We developed an online version in which participants foraged across four visual fields for (fictive) coins while risking aversive auditory screams. Each search field was associated with a specific combination of reward and punishment magnitude (low/high reward $\times$ low/high punishment), and these contingencies were explicitly instructed prior to the task. In each trial, participants decided whether and for how long to search within a field.

The task design allowed us to capture AAC during active exploration and examine decision policies under explicitly known reward–punishment contingencies. Specifically, for 46 participants, we quantified behavior at two levels: the binary commitment to search in a field captured whether participants approached a field at all, whereas the extent of search within a field indexed how far they were willing to pursue rewards under risk. Both click-related measures systematically varied with reward–punishment structure, being highest for high-reward/low-punishment states and lowest in the reverse condition, with a gradual decline across trials suggestive of fatigue.

To dissociate decision strategies, we implemented an agent-based behavioral modeling framework comparing alternative subjective value computations, including linear reward–punishment integration, non-linear reward–punishment interaction, approach bias, and trial drift effects. Formal model comparison indicated that commitment to search was best explained by agents integrating rewards and punishments with approach bias and trial-dependent decline, while the extent of the search additionally required sensitivity to reward–punishment interactions. We observed strong individual differences; preliminary analyses indicated that approach bias was positively associated with self-reported approach motivation and the subjective valence of the reward. These findings highlight that avoidance in instructed conflicts reflects multiple interacting components and support the use of online paradigms for computational psychiatry.

title: Arousal–Attainability–Value: A Bounded Dynamical Model of Wanting with Progress
abstract: Momentary wanting is shaped by attentional amplification, deprivation, and perceived feasibility, yet unified dynamical formulations that are both interpretable and stable remain limited. We propose a bounded dynamical model in which (i) arousal functions as an attentional amplifier computed as a soft conjunction of salience, novelty, and proximity; (ii) attainability encodes a feasibility belief sensitive to progress cues (approach vs. retreat) and success history; and (iii) manifest value (wanting) emerges from an arousal-weighted blend of latent value (liking) and a need–feasibility drive, gated by smooth disengagement functions. The model is specified via first-order relaxation dynamics, clipping, and logistic gates to ensure boundedness and interpretability. We test the model via simulation studies and ablation tests across two controlled scenarios — progress manipulation and history manipulation — demonstrating signature phenomena such as progress asymmetry and learned suppression after repeated failure. We further outline simulation studies for need-cycle dynamics and multi-object competition to demonstrate satiation-driven wanting and contextual re-ranking. This work provides a minimal computational core for dynamical accounts of motivational value and a foundation for later empirical validation.

title: A systematic analysis of representations in artificial neural networks across hyperparameters
abstract: Artificial neural networks trained by backpropagation are useful tools for simulating human neural representations, yet their internal representational geometry remains poorly understood. Researchers often select model hyperparameters based on task performance, but this practice assumes that high accuracy implies biological relevance. However, if networks with comparable performance develop different internal structures, accuracy-based selection may lead to misleading comparisons with brain data. Building on prior studies, which have usually focused on single hyperparameters, we provide a systematic multi-factor analysis of representational variability using a fully crossed hyperparameter design. This study explored the influence of eight hyperparameters – batch size, hidden layer size, learning rate, nonlinearity, optimizer, L1 and L2 regularization, and weight initialization – on the representations learned by 1504 feedforward networks trained on a dual-task MNIST dataset. Using representational similarity analysis, we quantified the consistency of the representations of the networks. Spearman rank correlations between representational dissimilarity matrices revealed substantial representational variability (ρ = .55), which decreased when averaging across networks with identical hyperparameter configurations (ρ = .70), indicating that representational differences arose from both hyperparameter choices and training stochasticity (random initialization and batch sampling). In addition, application of principal component analysis suggested that activation function, hidden layer size, optimizer choice and learning rate had the largest influence on network representations. Together, these findings show that networks with comparable behavioral performance can develop substantially different internal representations as a function of hyperparameter choice. More broadly, the results demonstrate that hyperparameters matter for representational geometry in complex and interacting ways that are not fully captured by task performance alone. This suggests that implementation details can impact inferences on model-brain comparisons, as representational conclusions may vary across different hyperparameter settings.

title: How Local Lexical Distance, Surprisal, and Context-level Semantic Distance affect the N400 to THIEF: Metrics from Large Language Models Reveal Context-Dependent Reweighting
abstract:
Prior work indicates that both local lexical association and discourse-level constraints modulate the N400, but their relative contributions across contexts remain unresolved. We addressed this question using large language model (LLM)-derived predictors of single-trial N400 amplitude in two EEG experiments with matched prime--probe pairs. Predictors were (i) prime--probe cosine distance (local lexical distance), (ii) cosine distance between discourse context and probe embeddings (context-level semantic distance), and (iii) probe surprisal.
In Experiment 1, participants heard a spoken prime and then viewed a related or unrelated probe (*e.g.*, CLASS–SCHOOL *vs.* CLASS–THIEF). Unrelated probes elicited larger N400 amplitudes, and local lexical distance significantly predicted trial-level N400 variation.
Experiment 2 reused the same prime--probe words, but the prime was the sentence-final word of a two-sentence vignette designed to induce a causal inference (*e.g.*, “Lucy got off her bike and locked it to a post. The bike was gone when she came out of class.”). The probe was either lexically related to the sentence-final word (*e.g.*, SCHOOL) or the unstated causal inference (*e.g.*, THIEF; unrelated in Experiment 1, *causally related* in Experiment 2). In this discourse condition, lexically related probes elicited larger N400 amplitudes than causally related probes.
Model comparisons showed that surprisal provided the strongest single-predictor account of N400 variance. Context-level semantic distance explained additional variance beyond surprisal, whereas local lexical distance did not improve fit once surprisal and context-level distance were included. These results support a context-dependent reweighting account: under causal discourse constraints, N400 variance is better captured by discourse-level predictive/semantic metrics than by local lexical association alone, and highlight the distinct, non-redundant contributions made by surprisal and context-level semantic distance to N400 modulation.

title: Quantifying Entrainment Evidence: A Comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Approaches for Information Processing Pathway Maps
abstract: Information Processing Pathway Maps (IPPMs) offer a scalable framework for formalizing the complex sequence of mathematical transformations applied to sensory stimuli. These maps chart the latency and cortical expression of computational steps, relying on statistical inference to link model outputs with observed neural activity. Traditionally, this mapping has relied on frequentist hypothesis testing. However, determining which of several competing computational models best explains neural data is a problem of model adjudication, arguably better suited to probabilistic inference. Here, we present a direct comparison between the established frequentist approach and a novel Bayesian framework for mapping cortical entrainment. While the Bayesian formulation retains the core strength of IPPMs—generating explicit predictions of time-varying neural signals—it fundamentally alters the selection criterion, shifting from rejecting a null hypothesis to quantifying the relative evidence for competing computational hypotheses. We evaluate the performance and interpretability of both approaches using an auditory neuroimaging dataset to reconstruct a known loudness-processing pathway. We discuss the implications of this shift for systems neuroscience, specifically regarding the handling of collinear models and the robust accumulation of evidence.

title: Multi-View Temporal Alignment for Cross-Species fMRI
abstract:
Cross-species neuroimaging is critical for linking cellular-resolution findings in non-human primates to human brain function. However, comparisons are complicated by differences in brain organization, behavior, and imaging signals. In particular, macaques are typically scanned using monocrystalline iron oxide nanoparticles (MION), which improves signal-to-noise but produces a hemodynamic response that differs from the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response in humans. This confounds data-driven analyses that rely on temporal alignment between species.

Here, we introduce Multiview Temporal Alignment (MVTA), a multivariate method that directly aligns macaque MION signals to human BOLD. By learning the temporal transform from variance that is shared across species, MVTA avoids contamination from species-specific and idiosyncratic signals and outperforms approaches based on canonical hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) or voxel-space objectives.

We first validate MVTA using simulations by comparing four pipelines for handling cross-species temporal correspondence: 1) comparisons of representational structure without temporal alignment (baseline), 2) an existing ``double convolution'' approach that involves convolving the observed data in each species with the canonical HRF of the other, 3)  a temporal transform learned from voxel space, and 4) MVTA. MVTA outperforms all other methods across several metrics.

We demonstrate how MVTA can be combined with hyperalignment to identify shared cross-species representational structure using a novel fMRI dataset in which macaques (3T, $n=3$) and humans (7T, $n=9$) viewed identical movies and functional localizers. Using human ROIs as seeds, we identified corresponding macaque regions: V1 to V1, face-selective regions to face-selective regions, and V4 overlapping ventral portion of its standard atlas definition (Jung et al., 2021). This pipeline provides a quantitative measure of cross-species 
representational correspondence under naturalistic stimulation. By improving temporal alignment, MVTA enables exploratory cross-species analyses that were previously infeasible.

title: Quantifying information gain in narrative stimuli using open-source large language models
abstract: Narrative structure is central to human memory, scaffolding the consolidation of past experience into structured knowledge and shaping the encoding of to-be-remembered information. Further, narratively-structured stimuli increase neural signals of engagement and value relative to non-narrative stimuli, suggesting that humans may exhibit an inductive bias toward narratively-structured information. These two lines of research have recently been integrated into a theory proposing that narrative structure facilitates credit assignment in high-dimensional and temporally discontiguous state-spaces (Chen & Bornstein, 2024). Because credit assignment is a ubiquitous problem faced by cognitive agents, understanding how it is solved by humans can help advance understanding of how it can be solved by other agents. To do this, methods are needed for quantifying the time-evolving valuation of information as it unfolds within a narrative. A recently-developed computational metric called Sequentiality (Sap et al., 2022) appears to be a promising tool toward this end, but additional work is needed to assess its utility for applications to the question of credit assignment. This project addresses that gap by (1) creating and validating an open-source, ensemble-based implementation of Sequentiality, (2) systematically characterizing the role of prior knowledge in shaping Sequentiality values, and (3) establishing a direct empirical link between Sequentiality and human judgments of event importance and causal centrality. Expanding upon the findings of Sap et al. (2022), we show that Sequentiality values critically depend on the prior knowledge an observer has about narrative structure. We suggest these findings motivate interpreting the metric in terms of $\textit{contextual information gain}$, rather than the original interpretation of schema-consistency or familiarity. Together, these findings pave the way for using Sequentiality as a proxy for a key theoretical construct involved in solving the credit assignment problem: an eligibility trace indicating which previous states are most relevant for updating or retrieving based on incoming information from the environment.

title: Could a neuroscientist understand a high-dimensional representation?
abstract: Understanding how neural systems process information requires analytical tools that can characterize their internal representations to the full extent. Brains and deep neural networks represent information in population codes, with stimulus-related variance distributed as a power-law over at least thousands of principal components (PCs). Can common modeling techniques in neuroscience fully characterize such representations? We first address this question by analyzing synthetic data matrices generated from power-law representations. We focus on representational similarity analysis (RSA) and encoding models, widely used techniques that have been proposed as preferred methods to compare representations. We show that when data are generated from power-law representations, like those seen in brains and DNNs, RSA and encoding scores are determined almost entirely by a handful of leading PCs and are insensitive to the bulk of the ground-truth components that make up the representation. In contrast, alternative approaches involving cross-validated orthogonal decomposition reveal reliable signal spanning multiple orders of magnitude of PCs. We next show that similar results are obtained when we apply the same analyses to a large-scale dataset of human fMRI responses to natural scenes, thus demonstrating that the limitations of RSA and encoding models characterized here have practical implications for analyses of real neuroscience data. Together, these findings reveal major limitations of common modeling techniques for characterizing population codes in high dimensions. More broadly, they suggest that the prevailing paradigms of the field are biased toward low-dimensional theories and may limit our ability to understand neural representations in their full complexity.

title: Is This the Real Life? Is This Just Fantasy? A Domain Adaptation Framework for Identifying Higher-Order Reality Representations
abstract: How does your brain know what’s real? Neural responses to perceived versus imagined content often seem to overlap in their neuroanatomical loci and representational structure, but the brain is nevertheless able to differentiate between imagery and perceptual input. How does the brain engage in this reality monitoring capacity, and what can this tell us about the mechanisms behind the conscious experience of seeing? A class of theories of consciousness, known as Higher-Order (HO) theories, posit that conscious experience depends on the formation of higher-order representations, which monitor and interpret first-order (perceptual and imagined) representations. Yet HO theories differ in their positioning on the nature of such HO representations. Here, we develop and validate a computational approach to interrogating the nature of HO representations by using domain adaptation (DA), a machine learning technique that can statistically align distributions of data from different sources. We apply DA to ask when and where patterns of human fMRI BOLD responses (N=18) can be aligned across perception and imagination, and across contents, to reveal areas that encode content-agnostic reality signals, reality-agnostic content signals, and signals of one type that are conditioned on the other, thereby providing differential support for specific aspects of competing HO theories. We find content-conditioned reality signals in the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex, while content-agnostic reality signals appear more in the occipital fusiform and occipital pole. In contrast, content representations specific to perception versus imagination appeared in the precuneus and intracalcarine cortex, while the temporal occipital fusiform cortex appeared to encode content regardless of its source. These results suggest highly localized and separable computations may collectively drive the overall assessment of whether an internal representation is real or imagined. Further, these results demonstrate the viability, promise, and power of DA approaches to interrogating the inputs to higher-order neural representations.

title: An Analysis of Neuroidal Memory Formation within D. melanogaster
abstract: The Neuroidal model poses a neurobiologically plausible theory for modeling the brain. This symbolic network has been shown to capture realistic memorization behaviors using the JOIN algorithm. The model has also been recently improved by incorporating Watts-Strogatz small-worlds within its base structure. From the efforts of neuroscience researchers, we have access to the Drosophila melanogaster ($\textit{D. melanogaster}$) fruit fly's connectome, which has been found to also contain small-worlds in this thesis. By synthesizing the Ocellar Ganglion (OCG) region of Drosophila, we compare a digitized version of a real-world brain with an instance of the Neuroidal model. In this thesis, we offer novel results that display the stability of JOIN within OCG, and a striking comparative evaluation between the Neuroidal model and OCG's capacity for memories. This study further establishes the Neuroidal model as both an efficient and plausible neural network for general cognition.

title: Predicting Human Visual Attention on Words in Source Code
abstract: This paper presents a computational model to predict human visual attention over words in software source code.  The visual attention of software engineers when reading source code has long been studied as a means to understand human cognitive processes during software engineering tasks.  Predicting this visual attention is important for perfecting user interface design and understanding what information human programmers need.  We propose a model of programmer visual attention in which we design a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention measured during eye tracking experiments and the internal attention of the artificial neural network.  We evaluate our model by comparing its outputs to actual eye tracking data from three separate datasets. Two are in the Java programming language and one is in the C programming language.  We find that our model outperforms relevant baselines by 39%, 82%, and 12% in each of these studies according to accepted metrics.

title: Task-conditioned neural dynamics reveal the computations underlying flexible face perception
abstract: Computational visual neuroscience seeks to identify the computations by which the brain dynamically categorizes the visual world and constructs social meaning. Humans rapidly infer identity and emotion from faces, yet it is unclear which computational operations selectively weigh, route and integrate static and dynamic features to support distinct categorization goals, and how these operations impose constraints on artificial neural network architectures. Here, we combine generative face modeling, with magnetoencephalography (MEG; n = 24) and information-theoretic analyses to derive stimulus feature representations directly from dynamic brain activity. We show that identity and emotion features are preserved and transmitted through distinct cortical pathways depending on task demands. Crucially, these feature streams converge in anterior temporal cortex, where static and dynamic features are nonlinearly and synergistically integrated into a person-specific representation that emerges only for familiar faces. Together, these results specify a task-conditioned computational mechanism–feature gating, pathway-specific routing, and nonlinear integration–that constructs social meaning and imposes concrete constraints on artificial neural network architectures, linking neural dynamics, cognition, and algorithmic models within a cognitive computational neuroscience framework. The empirical mechanisms underlying these findings are reported in a companion manuscript under review; the present work focuses on their computational interpretation and implications for cognitive computational neuroscience.

title: Brain Foundation Model Representations of Naturalistic Emotional Dynamics
abstract:
Emotional experience emerges from coordinated activity across distributed intrinsic brain networks, yet modeling these large-scale and temporally evolving patterns remains challenging with conventional neuroimaging approaches. Brain foundation models pretrained on large-scale fMRI datasets may provide a lower-dimensional representation space that supports decoding and interpretation of affective variables without requiring task-specific supervision.

Here, we evaluate this hypothesis using BrainLM, a masked-autoencoder transformer pretrained on large-scale fMRI recordings. We test whether its embeddings contain information associated with emotion-related variables during naturalistic movie viewing. Using leave-one-subject-out Ridge regression on both frozen and LoRA-finetuned embeddings, we predict continuous valence, arousal, and categorical emotion labels, and compare performance to linear and nonlinear models trained directly on parcel-level brain activity. BrainLM embeddings support comparable predictive performance while requiring only simple linear decoding, suggesting that they provide a compact and informative latent space for affective analysis.

To examine how this information is organized, we extend a perturbation-based interpretability framework to quantify how minimal changes in parcel-level input signals shift the learned embedding along affective dimensions. This yields parcel-level sensitivity estimates that identify regions contributing most strongly to changes in BrainLM embeddings. We then summarize interactions among high-sensitivity parcels using sparse weighted graphs and standard graph metrics, providing an interpretable view of how affect-related information is distributed across intrinsic brain networks. Valence-related shifts involve a smaller set of parcels within visual, salience, and executive networks, whereas arousal-related shifts engage a broader set spanning multiple networks. These graphs reflect co-variation in embedding sensitivity rather than direct functional connectivity, offering a complementary perspective on how the model integrates information across brain regions.

Together, these findings indicate that pretrained BrainLM embeddings can be used to examine both region- and network-level contributions to emotion-related representations. This approach provides an additional framework for exploring how distributed brain activity patterns are captured within foundation model embedding spaces.

title: Parameter-Efficient Alignment of VLM to Human Odd-One-Out Behavior
abstract:
Odd-one-out triplet tasks are widely used to derive a dimensional representation of object concepts from behavioral data, either for directly probing conceptual structure or for downstream uses. However, fitting behavioral embedding models typically requires millions of judgments and yields static representations that are costly to extend to new objects, or new stimulus images of known objects. This situation has motivated an interest in using machine learning foundation models to extrapolate beyond the original stimulus set, with the main constraints being cost and degree of alignment with human representations. 

In this work, we introduce a parameter-efficient feature compression method that aligns a pretrained vision--language model (CLIP) to human odd-one-out behavior by learning only a small head on top of fixed visual embeddings. The resulting low-dimensional representations achieve near-human accuracy on triplet prediction, and improve zero-shot generalization to novel objects and novel stimulus images relative to the pretrained baseline. Furthermore, they display closer agreement with the structure derived from human behavioral data using VICE, and the categorical organization of the objects considered. The same framework can be fine-tuned with small individualized triplet datasets to better capture subject-specific judgment patterns.

These results suggest that a simple, portable adaptation of an existing foundation model can serve as an accessible surrogate for human judgments in triplet tasks. More broadly, they support the view that modeling human behavior in this setting does not require using the largest foundation models, but can be achieved with compact, researcher-friendly tools.

title: How Do You Know It’s Real? Controlling False Positives in Whole-Brain Neural Decoding
abstract:
Contemporary work in functional brain imaging often suggests that neuro-cognitive representations can be widely distributed across many regions. Whole-brain neural decoding seeks to uncover such representational systems by using regularized machine learning to select features and decode activation patterns measured across the entire cortex. A central challenge for this approach concerns reliability: while standard cross-validation techniques will ensure that selected neural features (e.g. voxels, electrodes, etc) do jointly encode the targeted information, spurious correlations present in large and noisy datasets can nevertheless lead such models to also select many arbitrary features. How can we be sure the neural signals uncovered do not contain many such false positives?

To answer this question we introduce Knockoff-Max, a resampling-based false positive control framework, and evaluate its effectiveness when combined with a recently proposed whole-brain decoding method, Iterated LASSO (iLASSO). Simulation experiments with controlled ground-truth signals show that the integrated approach maintains false positive rates under 0.05, across different noise levels. When used to decode stimulus category (face, place or object) in an existing fMRI dataset, Knockoff-Max selects fewer features than iLASSO alone, but still discovers widely distributed representations spanning all four lobes of the brain. The results suggest that inclusive whole-brain decoding can reveal reliable distributed semantic neural representations even when false positives are stringently controlled, and offers a new technique for investigating whole-brain distributed codes in other domains.

title: Temporal Processing during Decision-Making under Uncertainty
abstract: Time perception and decision-making are interrelated processes that are critical to much of human and animal behavior. Although the behavioral importance of this link between the processes has been established, the neural underpinnings of temporal decision-making are unclear. The current study leverages human intracranial electrophysiology to investigate the neural contribution of temporal processing to decision-making under risk. To probe temporal decision-making, we use a version of the Balloon Analogue Risk Task, in which participants inflate virtual balloons with the goal of reaching maximal balloon size but stopping inflation before the balloon pops. Points are awarded based on inflation duration of successful trials, such that points awarded are linearly related to balloon size. By decoding temporal features of the task on a trial-by-trial basis, we find neural representations of time during balloon inflation. Specifically, we find that both medial and lateral temporal regions of the brain encode the majority of this time-related signal. Importantly, we can decode the progression of time leading up to the outcome of a successful decision (pressing a button to stop inflation before the balloon pops). This encoding of time depends on an active decision to end the trial: we cannot decode time during passive observation of balloon inflation to a known maximal size. To validate these results further, we used a temporal convolution network to predict participants’ response (i.e., time of button press) based on the brain activity leading up to the response. We found that we could predict the moment of response with high accuracy and temporal resolution. The model predicted the timing of successful decisions but not the timing of balloon pops. Together, these findings reveal neural representations that encode the progression of time, specifically in relation to an active decision.

title: Investigating Human–AI Alignment in Abstract Reasoning via Mechanistic interpretability
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) exhibit increasingly sophisticated problem-solving abilities, it remains unclear whether their internal computations align with human cognition. Recent correlational work found representational alignment between human neural activity and intermediate LLM layers during an abstract pattern completion task. To investigate whether these aligned representations causally drive behavior, we applied attribution patching to Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to isolate a sparse circuit of "consensus" attention heads that generalize across abstract pattern types. We then performed targeted causal ablations, comparing the effects on the model's predictions through its stack of layers against rigorous statistical controls. Ablating these consensus heads significantly reduced the model’s confidence in the correct solution token, an effect that was uniform across pattern types. Crucially, this circuit was localized in relatively late layers, diverging from prior intermediate-layer correlational findings. While preliminary, this divergence suggests that RSA and causal attribution methods may simply be sensitive to different aspects of the model's computation. Based on these results, we hypothesize that LLMs might process abstract reasoning in stages: utilizing intermediate layers for broad representational abstraction, while relying on late layers for task-agnostic output calibration. Further research is needed to fully disentangle these mechanisms.
